title: Port Mapping & Exposing Services 🚪
description: Master `-p`, `-P` and understand how traffic flows from host to container.

slides.title: The Container Network Is Private 🔐
slides.content:
# Why Port Mapping?

By default, containers on a bridge network have private IPs. The host cannot reach a web server running on container port 80 unless you explicitly open a door.

Port mapping creates a **DNAT** (Destination Network Address Translation) rule on the host, forwarding traffic from a host port to the container’s port.

Syntax:
```bash
docker run -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT IMAGE
```

slides.title: `-p` Examples 📝
slides.content:
# Common Port Mapping Patterns

- Map 8080 on host to 80 in container:
  `-p 8080:80`
- Map to a specific host interface:
  `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` (only localhost)
- Map multiple ports:
  `-p 8080:80 -p 443:443`
- Use `-P` to publish all EXPOSEd ports to random high ports on the host (10000+).

> The container must be listening on the container port for mapping to work.

quizData.question: In `-p 9090:80`, which port is accessed by the browser on the host?
quizData.explanation: The first number is the host port, the second is the container port. So 9090 on the host maps to 80 inside.

slides.title: Mapping Demo 🎬
slides.content: Run an Nginx container and access it from your browser:
slides.codeSnippet:
docker run -d --name nginx-host -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
# Open http://localhost:8080

# Check the mapping with docker port
docker port nginx-host
# Output: 80/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:8080

slides.title: Firewall & iptables 🔥
slides.content:
# How Docker Does It

Docker manipulates the host’s `iptables` to create NAT rules. When traffic hits the host port, it is forwarded to the container’s IP and port.

- You don’t need to configure firewalls manually for `-p` (Docker handles it).
- On Linux, local firewall (like ufw) may block; ensure Docker’s rules are allowed.

> Be careful: Binding to `0.0.0.0` makes the service available to the whole network (unless you bind to localhost).

quizData.question: Mapping a port with `-p 80:80` makes the container’s port 80 accessible from outside the host machine.
quizData.explanation: Unless you bind to a specific interface, Docker will bind to `0.0.0.0`, making the port available on all network interfaces.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use `docker port` to Verify
After starting a container with `-p`, run `docker port <container>` to see the exact mapping. It’s very useful for debugging.
